title: Exploring the Iris Dataset with R
text:
Introduction
The Iris dataset is a classic dataset used in statistics and data analysis. It contains measurements of iris flowers from three species:

Setosa
Versicolor
Virginica

The dataset is included in R, making it convenient for a reproducible analysis.


Load packages and data

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

data(iris)


iris_summary <- iris |>
  group_by(Species) |>
  summarise(
    mean_sepal_length = mean(Sepal.Length),
    mean_sepal_width = mean(Sepal.Width),
    mean_petal_length = mean(Petal.Length),
    mean_petal_width = mean(Petal.Width)
  )

iris_summary

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  Species  mean_sepal_length mean_sepal_width mean_petal_length mean_petal_width
  <fct>                <dbl>            <dbl>             <dbl>            <dbl>
1 setosa                5.01             3.43              1.46            0.246
2 versico…              5.94             2.77              4.26            1.33 
3 virgini…              6.59             2.97              5.55            2.03 




Summary statistics
I calculated the mean sepal length, sepal width, petal length, and petal width for each iris species.

ggplot(
  iris,
  aes(
    x = Sepal.Length,
    y = Petal.Length,
    colour = Species
  )
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Iris species comparison",
    x = "Sepal length (cm)",
    y = "Petal length (cm)",
    colour = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Sepal length versus petal length for the three iris species.





The visualization shows a clear separation between Setosa and the other two species based on petal length. Versicolor and Virginica have more similar measurements and show some overlap.


Discussion
This analysis demonstrates how R, dplyr, and ggplot2 can be used together in a Quarto document. The calculations and figure are generated when the document is rendered, making the analysis reproducible.


Data source
Data: Iris dataset, included with R as the built-in iris dataset. The dataset is documented in the R documentation for the datasets package.

title: Exploring the Iris Dataset with Python
text:
Introduction
The Iris dataset is a classic dataset in machine learning and statistics. It contains measurements of iris flowers from three species:

Setosa
Versicolor
Virginica

The dataset is included in the scikit-learn package, making it easy to use for exploratory analysis.


Load packages and data

from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


iris = load_iris()

df = pd.DataFrame(
    iris.data,
    columns=iris.feature_names
)

df["species"] = iris.target
df["species"] = df["species"].map({
    0: "setosa",
    1: "versicolor",
    2: "virginica"
})

The table above shows the average flower measurements for each species.


Visualization

plt.figure(figsize=(6,4))

for species in df["species"].unique():
    subset = df[df["species"] == species]
    plt.scatter(
        subset["sepal length (cm)"],
        subset["petal length (cm)"],
        label=species
    )

plt.xlabel("Sepal length (cm)")
plt.ylabel("Petal length (cm)")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Iris species comparison")

plt.show()







Figure 1: Sepal length versus petal length for the three iris species.







Discussion
The scatter plot shows differences among the three iris species. Setosa is separated from the other species, while Versicolor and Virginica overlap somewhat.
This analysis demonstrates how Python, pandas, matplotlib, and scikit-learn can be combined inside a Quarto document to perform a reproducible data analysis.


Data source
